name: Non-incisional double eyelid (suture method)

lead: The suture method creates an upper-lid crease by passing buried stitches through the eyelid, tethering skin to deeper tissue without a skin incision. The payoff is a defined double eyelid and a more open-looking eye, with the appeal of no cut.

Surgical papers describe it as one of two main approaches, the other being the incision method, and as very popular in Asia, especially China. Studies are retrospective cohorts and case series that look at how long creases last, reoperation risk by age and fat removal, and eyebrow position changes.

paras: Sutures are placed at one or more points (for example two-point or continuous techniques) and buried, creating an adhesion that forms the crease line. The crease is visible soon after the procedure, then settles as swelling goes down.

Because it leaves suture thread in the lid, foreign-material complications must be considered. Reports describe suture exposure causing corneal damage, sometimes initially misdiagnosed, crease loss from suture loosening and reoperation, and suture problems needing removal.

chain: Upper lid folds at the crease
angle.text: The suture method creates an upper-lid crease with buried stitches instead of an incision, giving a defined double eyelid soon after the procedure. It is popular in Asia, especially China. The literature focuses on how long the crease lasts and on suture complications.

lead: Non-incisional (buried suture) double eyelid surgery creates an upper-lid crease by placing stitches through the lid rather than cutting skin. Surgical papers describe it as one of two alternative approaches, the other being the incision method, and as very popular in Asia, especially China.[1][2][3]

Because it implants suture thread, authors say foreign-material complications must be considered.[3] Recent literature examines crease loss, reoperation risk by age and fat removal, and eyebrow position changes.[4][5][6][7][8]
The studies located are retrospective cohorts and case series.

paras: Variants in the literature include two-point buried suture,[8] continuous buried suture,[5] hidden non-incisional suture,[4] and orbicularis-levator-tarsus fixation suturing.[9] Two modified techniques were proposed to reduce complications specific to buried sutures.[3]

The HIROSHIMA Study, a high-volume retrospective observational study, used multivariate analysis to examine crease loss after hidden non-incisional suture surgery.[4] Other retrospective cohorts compared one-year outcomes in 788 cases between younger and older patients,[5] examined reoperation after upper eyelid fat removal over 4.5 years,[7] and analysed age-related reoperation risk from suture loosening.[8]

A Japanese series of 210 upper lids described suture-related complications and compared removal techniques.[1] Chinese series report corneal injury and conjunctival complications from exposed sutures, with one 14-patient study describing misdiagnosis before correct identification.[2][10]
A 2026 report examined eyebrow position changes after double eyelid surgery in relation to preoperative compensatory brow elevation.[6]

Evidence found is retrospective: complication series,[1][2][3][10] and recent cohort analyses of durability and reoperation.[4][5][7][8] No randomised comparison of suture and incision methods was found in the sources reviewed.
